chapters.title: AWS IAM (Identity and Access Management)
points: AWS IAM helps you securely control access to AWS services and resources
Users: an individual identity with permanent credentials
Groups: a collection of users; permissions are assigned to groups
Roles: an identity you can assume to get temporary permissions
Policies: JSON documents that define permissions
Permissions: Allow or Deny access to AWS resources
Authentication = Who are you? (proving your identity); Authorization = What can you do? (access permissions)
Flow: User -> Authentication (Login) -> Authorization -> AWS Resources
Root user is created with the AWS account and has full access to all AWS services
Best practice: do not use root user for daily activities; enable MFA for root user
MFA adds an extra security layer and requires 2 or more verification methods
MFA types: Virtual MFA (authenticator app), Hardware MFA (YubiKey), SMS MFA

chapters.title: IAM Policies and Permissions
points: Least privilege principle: grant only the minimum permissions necessary to perform the job
Least privilege reduces risk and improves security
IAM policy structure: Version, Statement block, Effect, Action, Resource
Policy example: {"Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [{"Effect": "Allow", "Action": ["s3:ListBucket", "s3:GetObject"], "Resource": ["arn:aws:s3:::my-bucket/*"]}]}
Version = policy version; Statement = statement block; Effect = Allow or Deny; Action = actions; Resource = resources
Policy effect Allow grants permission; Deny explicitly blocks access
How IAM works: User/Role requests AWS -> IAM checks policy -> Access Allowed or Denied
Roles give temporary credentials instead of long-term keys
Resources are identified by ARN (Amazon Resource Name) such as arn:aws:s3:::my-bucket/*

chapters.title: EC2 - Compute (Elastic Compute Cloud)
points: Amazon EC2 provides resizable compute capacity in the cloud; launch virtual servers (instances) and run applications
AMI (Amazon Machine Image): pre-configured template to launch an instance
Instance: virtual server running in AWS; you can start, stop, reboot it
Instance types: different types for different needs, e.g. t2.micro, m5.large, c6i.large
On-Demand: pay for what you use by the second or hour; Reserved: pay upfront for 1 or 3 years and get discount
Spot instances: unused EC2 capacity at a lower price, can be interrupted
Security Group acts as a virtual firewall; Key Pair used to securely connect (SSH); User Data is a script that runs on first start; Tags are key-value pairs to organize resources
Instance lifecycle: Pending (being created) -> Running -> Stopped (you pay for EBS) -> Terminated (deleted permanently)
Note: Stopped is not Terminated; a stopped instance can be started again

Pricing options: On-Demand (flexible pay as you go), Reserved (1 or 3 year commitment), Spot (up to 90% cheaper), Dedicated Hosts (physical server), Savings Plans (commit usage 1 or 3 years), Capacity Reservations (reserve in advance)
Storage options: EBS persistent block storage attached to instance; Instance Store temporary (lost on stop/terminate); EFS shared file storage for Linux; S3 object storage not mounted as block
Simple architecture: Users -> Internet -> Security Group -> EC2 Instance (with Elastic IP) -> Database and S3 inside AWS Cloud
Use cases: web servers, application servers, backend services, batch processing

chapters.title: EC2 - Advanced
points: Advanced features and services that work with EC2 to build highly available and scalable applications
EBS: persistent block storage for EC2; data is safe even if instance stops; types gp3 (General Purpose), io1/io2 (Provisioned IOPS), st1 (HDD), sc1 (Cold HDD); snapshots are backups of EBS
Elastic IP: static public IPv4 address that remains the same after instance restarts; can be associated and disassociated (example 203.0.113.10)

Auto Scaling: automatically adjusts EC2 capacity based on conditions (CPU, network, custom metrics); helps cost optimization and high availability; scaling policies increase or decrease the Auto Scaling Group
Load Balancing: distributes traffic across multiple instances; improves availability and reliability; types ALB (Application), NLB (Network), CLB (Classic)
Launch Templates: blueprints for launching EC2; include AMI, instance type, key pair, security group, user data, EBS volumes; used by Auto Scaling and EC2 Fleet
Placement Groups control how instances are placed on hardware: Cluster (low latency), Spread (high availability), Partition (large distributed apps like HDFS, Kafka)
Security Groups recap: virtual firewall, stateful so return traffic is allowed, allow/deny rules, applied at instance level, inbound and outbound rules
Key Pair: used for SSH access; public key stored by AWS, private key (.pem) you download and keep secure

Load balancer comparison: ALB Layer 7 (HTTP/HTTPS), HTTP/HTTPS/WebSocket, good performance; NLB Layer 4 (TCP/UDP), TCP/UDP/TLS, very high performance; CLB Layer 4 and 7, HTTP/HTTPS/TCP, low (legacy) performance
Important tip: use the right combination of EC2 features to build secure, scalable, highly available applications

chapters.title: S3 - Object Storage
points: Amazon S3 (Simple Storage Service) is an object storage service offering industry-leading scalability, data availability, security and performance
Stores data as objects inside buckets; each object consists of data, metadata and a unique key; access through Console, CLI or SDK
Object metadata: key, size, type, last modified
S3 Standard: general purpose, frequent access, low latency, high durability
S3 Intelligent-Tiering: automatic cost optimization, moves data between tiers automatically
S3 Standard-IA (Infrequent Access): lower cost, infrequent access, retrieval charges
S3 One Zone-IA: lower cost, data in a single Availability Zone, recreated if AZ destroyed
S3 Glacier: very low cost archival storage, retrieval takes minutes to hours; S3 Glacier Deep Archive: lowest cost, retrieval takes hours, long-term archive
Bucket features: global namespace (bucket names unique worldwide), versioning, lifecycle rules (auto transition or delete), encryption at rest (SSE-S3, SSE-KMS, CSE-KMS), bucket policies, CORS
Data consistency: strong read-after-write consistency for PUTs and DELETEs; list operations strongly consistent; latest data always returned
Access methods: AWS Management Console, AWS CLI, AWS SDK (language APIs), REST API

Security: IAM policies control who can access S3; bucket policies set permissions at bucket level; encryption in transit and at rest; MFA Delete for versioned buckets; Block Public Access prevents public exposure
Key features: highly scalable (unlimited data), highly durable (99.999999999% eleven nines), highly available (99.99%), cost effective (pay for what you use), high throughput and low latency
Common use cases: backup and restore, data archiving, static website hosting, big data analytics, media hosting, disaster recovery

chapters.title: AWS Database Services
points: AWS provides a wide range of database services to store, manage and scale your data in the cloud
RDS: managed relational database; supports MySQL, PostgreSQL, MariaDB, Oracle, SQL Server; automated backups, patching, monitoring; Multi-AZ for high availability; read replicas for scaling reads
RDS architecture: Application -> RDS -> Read Replica and Read Replica
Amazon Aurora: MySQL and PostgreSQL compatible, high performance and availability, auto-scaling storage, up to 15 read replicas, Multi-AZ DB cluster
DynamoDB (NoSQL): fully managed, key-value and document, single digit millisecond latency, automatically scales, uses capacity units (RCU/WCU), durable and highly available
DynamoDB table example: Partition Key UserID, Sort Key OrderID, Attributes Name and Price; Partition Key + Sort Key = unique item
ElastiCache: in-memory data store; improves application performance; supports Redis and Memcached; used for caching, session store, leaderboards; sits between Application and Database/RDS

Database comparison: RDS relational, traditional apps, vertical + read replicas, best for web apps/ERP/CRM; Aurora relational cloud native, high performance apps, auto scaling + replicas, modern apps/SaaS; DynamoDB NoSQL key-value/document, large scale low latency, automatic scaling, mobile/IoT/gaming; ElastiCache in-memory cache, caching/session store, automatic, high speed apps

Backups and recovery (RDS and Aurora): automated backups enabled by default; manual snapshots on demand; Point-in-Time Recovery (PITR) restore to any second; cross-region snapshot for disaster recovery; flow Backup -> Snapshot -> Restore

DynamoDB key concepts: partition key determines partition; sort key sorts data within the same partition; indexes GSI (Global Secondary Index) and LSI (Local Secondary Index); all items with same PK stored together
When to use what: need ACID transactions -> use RDS/Aurora; need massive scale and low latency -> DynamoDB; need caching -> ElastiCache
Database best practices: use appropriate DB for the right use case, enable backups, use Multi-AZ, monitor performance

chapters.title: AWS VPC and Networking
points: Amazon VPC (Virtual Private Cloud) lets you launch AWS resources in a logically isolated network that you define
VPC is a virtual network dedicated to your AWS account; complete control over IP range, subnets, route tables and gateways; isolated from other VPCs; highly secure and scalable

VPC components: VPC (your virtual network), Subnet (range of IPs in a VPC), Route Table (rules determining where traffic is routed), Internet Gateway (VPC to internet), NAT Gateway (private subnet instances access internet), Security Group (stateful firewall for instances), Network ACL (stateless firewall for subnets)

Architecture example: VPC 10.0.0.0/16 with Availability Zone A and B; public subnets 10.0.1.0/24 and 10.0.2.0/24 with public EC2 reaching Internet via IGW; private subnets 10.0.3.0/24 and 10.0.4.0/24 with private EC2 via NAT GW; route table connects subnets
Public subnet has a route to Internet Gateway so resources are reachable from internet; private subnet has no direct route, access via NAT Gateway
Subnet use cases: public subnet for web servers, bastion host, load balancer; private subnet for application servers, databases, internal services
Route table example: 10.0.0.0/16 -> local; 0.0.0.0/0 -> Internet Gateway (public subnet); 0.0.0.0/0 -> NAT Gateway (private subnet)

Security Group vs Network ACL: SG is virtual firewall for EC2 at instance level, allow rules only, stateful, default allow all outbound, applies to ENI/instance, no rule order; NACL is virtual firewall for subnet, allow and deny rules, stateless, default deny all, applies to subnet, evaluated by rule number top to bottom
CIDR (Classless Inter-Domain Routing) defines the IP range of your VPC; example 10.0.0.0/16 = 65,536 IPs
Choose non-overlapping CIDR blocks across VPCs, e.g. VPC 1 10.0.0.0/16 and VPC 2 192.168.0.0/16
Best practices: use private subnets for databases and internal resources; use security groups to allow only necessary traffic; use NACLs for subnet-level control; enable VPC Flow Logs
Common use cases: host web applications in public subnets, secure databases in private subnets, hybrid cloud connectivity

chapters.title: AWS Networking - Advanced
points: AWS provides powerful networking services to connect resources, users and applications securely around the world
Route 53: scalable DNS web service; converts domain names to IP addresses; highly available and low latency; health checks, traffic routing, domain registration; www.example.com -> 53 -> 192.0.2.10
Elastic Load Balancing: automatically distributes incoming traffic across multiple targets; improves availability, fault tolerance and scalability; types ALB, NLB, GWLB, CLB

CloudFront (CDN): content delivery network with low latency and high transfer speeds; global edge locations cache content; DDoS protection, SSL/TLS, compression, geo-restriction; users worldwide -> edge locations -> S3/origin
VPC Peering: connects two VPCs privately over the AWS backbone; no transit gateway or internet gateway required; supports overlapping CIDR with caution; VPC A 10.0.0.0/16 <-> VPC B 10.1.0.0/16
Transit Gateway: central hub connecting multiple VPCs and on-premises networks; scales to thousands of VPCs; simplifies network management; supports inter-region peering
VPN Connection: connects on-premises network to AWS over the internet; encrypted tunnel using IPSec; types Site-to-Site VPN and Client VPN
AWS Direct Connect: dedicated network connection from on-premises to AWS; more consistent than internet; reduced bandwidth costs; higher throughput and security
Route 53 routing policies: Simple (single resource), Weighted (by weights), Latency (lowest latency region), Failover (active-passive), Geolocation (user location), Geoproximity (resources near user)
Public traffic flow: User -> Internet -> IGW -> EC2 in public subnet; private flow: instance in private subnet -> NAT Gateway -> internet
Network ACL vs Security Group: NACL stateless, subnet level, allow/deny; SG stateful, instance level, allow only

chapters.title: AWS Storage and File Services
points: AWS provides a variety of storage and file services to store, share and manage data securely and cost-effectively
EBS (Elastic Block Store): block level storage for EC2; persists independently of instance; high performance; types gp3, io1/io2, st1, sc1; use case databases and critical applications
S3 (Simple Storage Service): object storage; highly durable (11 9s); scalable and cost-effective; stores any amount of data; use cases backup, static website, data lake, archives
EFS (Elastic File System): managed file storage for Linux; shared across multiple EC2 instances; uses NFS (v4.1 and v4.2); use case content management, web serving
FSx: managed file systems for Windows, Lustre, NetApp; high performance and scalability; integrated with AWS services; use case Windows shares, HPC, enterprise apps

S3 storage classes table: Standard (frequent, 11 9s, 99.99%), Standard-IA (infrequent, 99.9%), One Zone-IA (recreatable, 99.5%), Glacier Instant (archive instant retrieval, 99.9%), Glacier Flexible (archive minutes-hours, 99.9%), Glacier Deep Archive (long term lowest cost, 99.9%); all 11 9s durability
Tip: choose the right storage class to optimize cost and performance based on access patterns

EBS volume types: gp3 general purpose (balanced performance and cost), io1/io2 high IOPS (mission critical), st1 throughput intensive (low cost high throughput, big data, logs), sc1 cold workloads (lowest cost, infrequent access)
Key takeaways: EBS block storage for EC2; S3 object storage for any data; EFS/FSx file storage for shared access; choose correct class/type to optimize cost; AWS storage is durable, secure, scalable
Quick recap: Block -> EBS, Object -> S3, File -> EFS/FSx

Storage comparison: EBS block, single AZ, not shared, N/A protocol, databases/OS; S3 object, internet, shared, HTTP, backups; EFS file, multi-AZ, shared, NFS, shared content; FSx file, shared, SMB/Lustre, Windows/HPC

chapters.title: AWS Security and IAM
points: AWS provides a shared responsibility model and a wide range of security services to protect resources, data and applications

Shared responsibility: AWS is responsible for security OF the cloud (data centers, hardware, networking, virtualization, managed services); customer is responsible for security IN the cloud (data, applications, OS and network config, access management, user permissions)
IAM manages access to AWS services securely; grant least privilege; use MFA; never use root account for daily tasks
IAM components: User, Group, Role, Policy, Credential
IAM policy is a JSON document defining permissions and restrictions; main elements Effect (Allow/Deny), Action (API/service), Resource (ARN), Condition (optional)
Policy example with condition: {"Effect": "Allow", "Action": ["s3:ListBucket"], "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::my-bucket", "Condition": {"IpAddress": {"aws:SourceIp": "203.0.113.0/24"}}}

Security best practices: enable MFA for all users; use IAM roles instead of long-term credentials; least privilege; rotate access keys; enable CloudTrail and monitor; encrypt at rest and in transit; use Security Groups and NACLs; keep resources updated

Key security services: IAM (users, groups, roles, policies), CloudTrail (records account activity and API calls for auditing), KMS (manage encryption keys), WAF (protects web apps from exploits), GuardDuty (threat detection using ML and anomaly detection)

Security Group vs NACL: SG stateful, instance level, allow rules only, default deny all, applies to EC2 instance, no order, return traffic automatically allowed; NACL stateless, subnet level, allow and deny, default allow all, applies to subnet, rule number 1-32766, return traffic must be allowed explicitly
Encryption options: data at rest (EBS, S3, RDS; use KMS), data in transit (SSL/TLS for all connections), key management (AWS KMS manages keys, rotate periodically)

Common mistakes: using root account daily, over-permissioned IAM policies, hardcoding access keys in code, not enabling MFA, not monitoring with CloudTrail/GuardDuty, leaving unused resources and open ports

chapters.title: AWS Management and Monitoring
points: AWS provides management and monitoring services to operate resources efficiently

CloudWatch: monitoring and observability service; collects metrics, logs and events; create dashboards and alarms; use cases performance monitoring, troubleshooting, alerting; architecture Metrics/Logs/Events -> CloudWatch -> Metrics, Logs, Alarms
CloudTrail: tracks API calls and account activity; audit logs for governance, compliance and security; logs delivered to S3 for long-term storage; flow API Call/Event -> CloudTrail -> S3 Bucket

AWS Config: monitors and records configuration changes; evaluates configurations against desired settings; compliance and change management; stores configuration history; workflow Resource Change -> AWS Config -> Evaluate Rules -> Store History (S3)
Systems Manager (SSM): manage and operate EC2 at scale; capabilities Session Manager (SSH without key), Parameter Store, Patch Manager, Run Command, Automation

CloudFormation: Infrastructure as Code (IaC); create and manage resources using JSON/YAML templates; consistency and repeatability; supports update, rollback and stack management; process Template -> CloudFormation Stack -> AWS Resources
Trusted Advisor: online tool to improve security, performance and cost optimization; checks across 5 pillars: Cost Optimization, Performance, Security, Fault Tolerance, Service Limits

EventBridge: serverless event bus; connects applications using events; sources AWS services, custom apps, SaaS; use cases event-driven architectures, automation; flow Event Source -> EventBridge (Event Bus) -> Targets (Lambda, SQS, SNS, more)

AWS Organizations: manage multiple AWS accounts centrally; create OUs (Organizational Units); apply policies using Service Control Policies (SCP); consolidated billing and access management; structure Management Account -> OUs -> AWS Accounts
Quick tips: use CloudWatch for monitoring and alerts; enable CloudTrail in all regions; use CloudFormation for repeatable infrastructure
Common use cases: monitor application health, audit account activity, automate infrastructure, manage multi-account setups

chapters.title: AWS Database Services (Deep Dive)
points: AWS offers fully managed database services for different use cases, workloads and performance needs
RDS: managed relational; MySQL, PostgreSQL, MariaDB, Oracle, SQL Server; automated backups, patching, monitoring; Multi-AZ high availability; use case web apps, ERP, traditional apps
RDS architecture: Application -> RDS Instance -> Storage (EBS); RDS Instance -> Standby (Multi-AZ) and Read Replica
DynamoDB: fully managed NoSQL; key-value and document; single-digit millisecond latency; auto scaling, high availability; use case gaming, ad tech, IoT, mobile apps
DynamoDB table example: Partition Key UserID -> Name, Email; OrderID -> Amount, Status; ProductID -> Price, Stock

Aurora: MySQL and PostgreSQL compatible; up to 5x performance of standard MySQL; auto scaling storage; Multi-AZ high availability; use case high performance apps; architecture Application -> Aurora Primary -> Aurora Storage, with two Aurora Replicas
Redshift: data warehouse for analytics; columnar storage for high performance; scales to petabytes; use case BI, reporting, data analysis; flow Data Sources -> Amazon Redshift -> BI/Analytics/Reports

ElastiCache: in-memory caching; Redis and Memcached; improves performance and reduces database load; use case session store, leaderboards, caching; architecture Application -> ElastiCache (Redis) -> Database
DocumentDB: MongoDB compatible document database; fully managed and highly available; auto scaling storage; use case content management, catalogs, mobile apps
DocumentDB document example: {"_id": "123", "name": "Abhi", "email": "abhi@example.com", "skills": ["AWS", "Docker"], "age": 25}

Database comparison: RDS relational (MySQL/PostgreSQL/MariaDB/Oracle/SQL Server, general purpose, Multi-AZ/read replicas/backups/patching); DynamoDB NoSQL (key-value/document, high scale low latency, serverless/auto scaling/single-digit ms); Aurora relational (MySQL/PostgreSQL, high performance, 5x/auto scaling/Multi-AZ); Redshift data warehouse (columnar, analytics/reporting/BI, petabyte scale); ElastiCache in-memory (Redis/Memcached, caching/session/real-time, microsecond latency); DocumentDB document (MongoDB, content/catalogs, managed/scalable)
Best practices: choose the right database for your workload; enable backups and monitor performance; encrypt at rest and in transit; apply least privilege; review and optimize costs regularly

chapters.title: AWS Compute Services
points: AWS provides a wide range of compute services, from simple VMs to serverless functions

EC2: virtual servers in the cloud; full control over OS, network and storage; multiple instance types and sizes; use cases web servers, applications, dev/test, databases; architecture User -> EC2 -> EBS Volume, with Security Group

Lambda: serverless compute; run code without managing servers; pay only for the time code runs; supports multiple runtimes; use cases microservices, file processing, automation; flow S3 Bucket -> Lambda Function -> DynamoDB

ECS (Elastic Container Service): fully managed container orchestration; supports Docker; easy deployment, scaling, management; use case containerized apps; architecture Docker -> ECS Cluster -> Task, with ECR registry
EKS (Elastic Kubernetes Service): managed Kubernetes; deploy, manage, scale clusters; high availability and security; use case Kubernetes workloads, microservices; architecture EKS Cluster -> Nodes
Lightsail: simplified VPS (Virtual Private Server); easy to launch; bundles include compute, storage, database, networking; use case small websites, blogs, dev environments

Batch: fully managed batch processing; runs batch jobs efficiently; automatically provisions resources; use case data processing, scientific simulations; flow Job Queue -> Compute Environment -> Job Complete

Compute comparison: EC2 virtual machines (you manage, full control); Lambda serverless (AWS manages, event-driven small tasks); ECS containers (AWS manages, Docker); EKS Kubernetes (AWS manages, K8s workloads); Lightsail VPS (AWS manages, small sites); Batch (AWS manages, large scale batch jobs)

Common use cases: EC2 web servers/legacy/custom software; Lambda image resizing/notifications/real-time processing; ECS microservices/containerized apps; EKS complex container orchestration with K8s; Lightsail small business sites/prototypes/dev-test; Batch data analysis/rendering/scientific workloads
Key takeaways: choose the right compute service based on workload; use Lambda for event-driven tasks; use containers for portability
Tip: start with EC2 for control, move to serverless and containers to reduce operational overhead

chapters.title: AWS Networking Services
points: AWS provides networking services to build secure, reliable and scalable applications in the cloud

VPC: isolated virtual network; you define IP range; complete control over networking; use cases secure environments, hybrid cloud, microservices; architecture VPC 10.0.0.0/16 -> Public Subnet 10.0.1.0/24 (Internet Gateway) and Private Subnet 10.0.2.0/24 (NAT Gateway)
Route 53: highly available scalable DNS; routes users to the right resources; health checking and failover; use cases DNS routing, latency routing, geo routing; flow User -> 53 -> Web Server
Elastic Load Balancing: distributes incoming traffic across targets; improves availability and fault tolerance; types ALB, NLB, Gateway LB; use case high traffic apps; architecture ELB -> Instance x3
CloudFront: CDN with low latency; global edge locations; use cases websites, streaming, APIs; flow User -> CloudFront Edge Location -> S3 Bucket

Direct Connect: dedicated network connection to AWS; more reliable, secure and faster; reduces internet traffic cost; use cases hybrid cloud, large data transfer; flow On-premise Network -> Direct Connect -> aws

VPN (Site-to-Site): secure encrypted connection over the internet; connects on-premise network to VPC; cost-effective; use cases remote offices, hybrid cloud; flow On-premise Network -> VPN Connection -> VPC

Networking comparison: VPC networking (isolated cloud network, all apps); Route 53 DNS (domain routing, web apps); ELB load balancer (distribute traffic, HA apps); CloudFront CDN (deliver content globally, websites/media); Direct Connect dedicated network (private connection, enterprise/hybrid); VPN encrypted network (secure over internet, remote offices)

Security in networking: use Security Groups for inbound/outbound; NACLs for subnet-level filtering; enable VPC Flow Logs; use AWS WAF with CloudFront and ALB; encrypt in transit (TLS) and at rest; private subnets for backend

Common use cases: build secure isolated network with VPC; route users to nearest instance with Route 53; handle millions of users with ELB; deliver static and dynamic content globally with CloudFront; establish dedicated connectivity with Direct Connect
Key takeaways: VPC is the foundation of your network; Route 53 helps users find resources; ELB ensures HA and scalability; CloudFront brings content closer to users

chapters.title: AWS Storage Services
points: AWS provides a range of storage services to store, secure and retrieve data in the cloud
S3: object storage; stores data in buckets as objects; highly durable, scalable, available; use cases backups, static websites, data lakes; structure Bucket -> Objects (files)
EBS: block storage for EC2 instances; persistent; use cases databases, boot volumes, enterprise apps; architecture EC2 Instance -> EBS Volume
EFS: managed file storage for Linux; shared across multiple EC2; use cases content management, web serving; architecture EFS File System -> EC2 Instances
FSx: managed file systems for Windows, Lustre, NetApp ONTAP, OpenZFS; high performance and fully managed; use cases HPC, media workflows, enterprise apps
S3 Glacier: low-cost archival storage for infrequently accessed data; options Instant Retrieval, Flexible Retrieval, Deep Archive; flow S3 Bucket -> Glacier Storage (Archive)
Storage Gateway: hybrid storage service connecting on-premise apps to cloud storage; types File Gateway, Volume Gateway, Tape Gateway; On-premise Application <-> AWS Cloud Storage

Storage comparison: S3 object, internet, 11 9s, backups/data lakes/static sites; EBS block, EC2 instance, 99.999% (4 9s), databases/boot/enterprise; EFS file (NFS), multiple EC2, 11 9s, content sharing/web; FSx file, VPC/on-prem, varies, HPC/Windows/media; S3 Glacier object archive, internet, 11 9s, long-term archive; Storage Gateway hybrid, on-prem/cloud, varies, hybrid integration

Key features summary: S3 highly scalable object storage; EBS block storage for EC2; EFS shared file storage; FSx fully managed high-performance file systems; S3 Glacier low-cost archival; Storage Gateway bridge between on-prem and cloud

S3 storage classes: Standard (frequent, low latency), Standard-IA (infrequent, lower cost), One Zone-IA (infrequent, single AZ), Glacier Instant (archive, instant retrieval), Glacier Flexible (archive, minutes to hours), Glacier Deep Archive (lowest cost, hours retrieval)

Best practices: choose the right storage service; enable versioning and lifecycle policies in S3; encrypt at rest and in transit; MFA delete for critical buckets; monitor storage usage and costs; regularly review access permissions
